source: Zheng, Goldwater & Gentner (2025) Structural alignment and linguistic contrast help children learn a key principle of spatial construction
finding: Experiment 1: a contrastive label (the brace label) helped 5-7 year olds on transfer. Alignment of training pairs also helped. No alignment x language interaction.
numbers: N=64 children (16 per cell). Transfer: language b=2.278, p=.001, OR 3.15 [1.63,6.88]; alignment b=1.938, p=.005, OR 2.66. Repair: alignment p=.003, OR 2.31; language ns (label came after repair). Mean repair high-align .78 vs low-align .41.
limits: Label was given after the repair task, so its effect is on transfer only. Boys beat girls on transfer (.83 vs .57). Small cells.
agent_relevance: Naming the key difference between two cases can help even when the cases are poorly aligned. Add a step: label the relation or difference, then compare.

source: Zheng, Goldwater & Gentner (2025) Structural alignment and linguistic contrast help children learn a key principle of spatial construction
finding: Experiment 2 replicated Exp 1 and tested a 2-5 day delay and far transfer. Label and alignment effects held after delay.
numbers: N=116 after exclusions (29 per cell; 136 recruited, 15 lost to attrition, 5 failed memory check). Day 2 repair: language OR 1.76 [1.14,2.79], p=.012; near transfer: language OR 2.57 [1.51,4.62], p=.001; far transfer construction: language OR 1.60, p=.027; far recognition: language OR 1.75, p=.007; alignment far construction ns (p=.15).
limits: Effects are modest (ORs 1.6-2.6). Brace principle only, one domain, US children. Label effect on far transfer exceeded alignment effect on one task.
agent_relevance: Labels carry over a delay and to far cases. This supports storing named relations in memory notes for reuse, not only in-context use.

source: Zheng, Goldwater & Gentner (2025) Structural alignment and linguistic contrast help children learn a key principle of spatial construction
finding: Reported review of older findings: common novel labels invite comparison; labelling stabilises relational concepts such as left/right.
numbers: As reported in the 2025 introduction: Dessalegn & Landau (2008) 57% correct without relational language vs 79% with 'red is on the left'. Gentner & Namy (1999): after two standards got the same novel label, 4-year-olds favoured the taxonomic match. Namy & Gentner (2002): different labels on the two standards led to perceptual-match choice.
limits: Second-hand figures taken from the 2025 introduction, not from the original papers.
agent_relevance: Same label on two cases is a cue to compare them. Different labels cue contrast. An agent can control this by choosing label reuse.

source: Zheng, Goldwater & Gentner (2025) Structural alignment and linguistic contrast help children learn a key principle of spatial construction
finding: Reported summary of Loewenstein & Gentner (2005) Exp 5 and Yuan et al. (2024): relational terms shape encoding and persist.
numbers: As reported: 3-year-olds given top/middle/bottom terms were above chance finding the analogous toy; controls at chance. Advantage persisted to new structures and a 2-day delay with only general language. Yuan et al. 2024 eye-tracking: relational phrase directed 4-year-olds' attention to bind colour to left/right, and benefit continued on later trials without language.
limits: Second-hand description. Preschool children, one spatial task family.
agent_relevance: Relational words work at encoding time (they shape the representation), not only at answer time. Naming early in S2 may matter more than naming late.

source: Zheng, Goldwater & Gentner (2025) Structural alignment and linguistic contrast help children learn a key principle of spatial construction
finding: Reported summary of Loewenstein & Gentner (2001) model-room studies: comparison, without any new word, raised relational mapping.
numbers: As reported: twin-object trials over 70% correct after a close comparison vs 42% in control. DeLoache (1989): 37.5% found the toy in the bigger room though 83% remembered the original location.
limits: Second-hand. Shows comparison alone does much of the work, so labels are one route among several.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation: part of the 'label effect' is the comparison it invites. Test label versus plain comparison in the agent.

source: Loewenstein & Gentner (2005) Relational language and the development of relational mapping
finding: Five experiments: spatial relational words (top, middle, bottom) improved preschoolers' mapping in a three-tier box, with effects at younger ages on easier tasks and older ages on harder tasks.
numbers: Abstract only: effects of language differed with term semantics (Exp 4); advantage held 2 days later (Exp 5). Cell numbers not read.
limits: Abstract only this session. Original numbers not verified.
agent_relevance: Founding study for the claim that named relations shape the encoding. Key for S2.

source: Jamrozik & Gentner (2020) Relational labeling unlocks inert knowledge
finding: Two studies with adults: giving relational labels at encoding or at retrieval raised cross-domain relational retrieval. Domain labels did not reliably help domain retrieval.
numbers: Abstract only. Retrieval rates and N not read.
limits: Abstract only. Retrieval of analogues from memory, not generation of new analogies.
agent_relevance: Direct support for an S2 step that names the relation of the current problem and uses that name as a retrieval key into stored cases.

source: Structure mapping and relational language support children's learning of relational categories (Child Development, 2011)
finding: Children 3, 4-5 and 6 years old extended relational categories (nest is home for bird) better when they heard a novel category name in a relational frame and compared members. 3-year-olds learned only with relational language plus progressive-alignment comparisons.
numbers: Abstract only. Cell sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only. Youngest children needed both factors.
agent_relevance: Label plus comparison, in a progressive order from close to far, is the strongest combination. Matches ordered case comparison in the schema.

source: Gentner (2016) Language as cognitive tool kit: How language supports relational thought
finding: Proposes that learning and using relational language fosters relational reasoning, a moderate Whorfian claim.
numbers: Abstract only.
limits: Review by the main proponent. Not independent evidence.
agent_relevance: Theory statement for S2 naming.

source: Are redundant labels helpful during category learning? Replication of Lupyan, Rakison & McClelland (2007), preprint 2026
finding: An online replication of Experiment 2 with adults failed to find that labelled learners learned the categories faster.
numbers: Abstract only: auditory or written label vs no label and non-linguistic cue. Sample size not read.
limits: Online replication, preprint, adults, subordinate categories. Abstract only. A failed replication of a core label-feedback result.
agent_relevance: Do not assume labels speed up learning of visually distinct categories. Test it in the agent.

source: Mind Melds: Verbal labels induce greater representational alignment (Open Mind, 2024)
finding: Experiment 1: redundant nonsense labels during a matching task made later free sorts more categorical and more aligned between people. Matching without labels did not.
numbers: Baseline N=45, No Labels N=43, With Labels N=41. Categoricality .65 (labels) vs .38 baseline (p=.024) and .40 no-labels (p=.038). Alignment .20 vs .11 and .12 (both p<.001). 2-cluster sorts 53% vs 20% and 33%. Match accuracy about .98 in both; RT slower with labels (692 vs 585 ms).
limits: Novel visual shapes, online adults. Labels redundant, so effect is on the representation, not on information.
agent_relevance: Names make different readers converge on the same categories. Shared names across sub-agents could align their representations.

source: Mind Melds: Verbal labels induce greater representational alignment (Open Mind, 2024)
finding: Experiment 2 replicated the alignment effect with more confusable shapes, but the cluster-number and categoricality effects were weaker.
numbers: N=122 (41 baseline, 37 no labels, 44 with labels). Alignment with labels M=.35. Categoricality .66 vs baseline .49 (p=.04), vs no labels .60 (ns). 2-cluster sorts 60% vs 37% and 35%. Mean clusters 2.8 vs 3.2 and 3.31 (ns). Match RT equal (773 vs 769 ms).
limits: Part of the effect did not replicate in the same paper: only alignment and 2-cluster rate were reliable. Same lab, within one paper.
agent_relevance: Label effects are real but small and partly fragile. Plan agent tests with enough items.

source: Categorization in infancy: labeling induces a persisting focus on commonalities (Developmental Science, 2016)
finding: Eye tracking of 12-month-olds: with labels, categorisation was linked to attention to shared features, and this focus persisted after learning without labels. Without labels, attention followed feature variability.
numbers: Abstract and introduction only read. Both groups learned the category. N and statistics not extracted.
limits: Infants, one novel category. Attention data, not later reasoning.
agent_relevance: Mechanism evidence: labels direct attention to what is shared across cases.

source: Lupyan & Ward (2013) Language can boost otherwise unseen objects into visual awareness (PNAS)
finding: Hearing a valid label before a continuous flash suppression trial improved detection. Invalid labels hurt. Effects were on d' and RT.
numbers: Abstract only. Exact d' values not read.
limits: Abstract only. This is perception, not relations, but it is the strongest claim that words change processing, and it is contested (next line).
agent_relevance: Extreme end of label effects. Treat as boundary, not as guidance for text agents.

source: Linguistic cues do not influence subliminal visual processing: an electrophysiological study (Cortex, 2026)
finding: Preregistered EEG study combining Lupyan & Ward (2013) and Sekar et al. (2013) found no label boost for unseen targets.
numbers: N=20. Congruent cues did not help unseen ('didn't see') targets. Incongruent cues impaired identification. No change in Visual Awareness Negativity amplitude or in proportion of unseen trials.
limits: Small N, abstract only. Argues earlier results may be post-perceptual. Supports a weaker view: labels bias later decisions.
agent_relevance: Label effects probably come from later stages (memory, decision), which is fine for an LLM agent.

source: The role of language in forming the concepts same and different (Cognition, 2026)
finding: Four-year-olds passed relational match-to-sample without training in three vertical conditions. Children who justified choices with relational language did better than those who did not.
numbers: Exp 1 N=79, Wilcoxon r >= .48; Exp 2 N=31, r=.62 (horizontal axis). Abstract only.
limits: Correlational for the language-justification link. Abstract only. Argues the concept same/different is the key, and language use is a better predictor than age.
agent_relevance: Production of a relational term is a marker of the concept. Ask the agent to state the relation before using it.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models, Nature Human Behaviour
finding: GPT-3 matched or beat UCLA undergraduates on text matrix, letter-string and four-term verbal analogy tasks, zero-shot.
numbers: Digit matrices: humans N=40, GPT-3 vs humans OR=1.88, p=.005. Letter strings: humans N=57, OR=1.76, p=6.3e-5. Verbal analogies: GPT-3 as good or better on UCLA VAT (N=57) and Sternberg and Nigro (N=20), above average SAT high-school level; Jones et al. dataset (N=241) in range but weaker. Semantic distance effect OR=3.24, p=.0165.
limits: GPT-3 level. Training-data exposure is a risk. Next line shows brittleness.
agent_relevance: Relation naming is already in model weights. Gain from explicit naming is likely about retrieval and consistency, not new capability.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: On letter-string analogies with permuted alphabets, GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 dropped sharply while humans stayed flat. The apparent human-level result did not hold on new problems.
numbers: Human samples per condition 268-384 (46 human samples for original problems vs 57 in Webb). Human accuracy about constant across 0, 2, 5, 10, 20 permuted letters; GPT models fall at each step and again for symbol alphabets. Comprehension checks were mostly passed. Humans in this study scored higher than Webb's humans on original problems; GPT models scored lower than humans on the original problems, unlike Webb.
limits: Prompt choice matters. Letter-string domain only. Exact accuracy values read from figures only qualitatively.
agent_relevance: Naming and applying a relation is tied to familiar surface forms. Test the agent with counterfactual relabelled domains.

source: Lee et al. (2025) The curious case of analogies: investigating analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Models encode the relation of the first pair in mid-upper layers when correct. Failures show missing relation information or failure to apply the relation to new entities. Patching hidden states helped some failures.
numbers: Patching fixes up to 38.4% of incorrect cases. Exp 1 gains: Llama-2-13B +32.3%, Gemma-7B +38.4%, Qwen2.5-14B +35.6%. Exp 2: +25.9%, +38.1%, +30.5%.
limits: Open-weight 7-14B models, proportional and story analogies. Patching is not available in a prompting-only agent.
agent_relevance: Applying a relation to new entities is as large a bottleneck as finding it. S2 should both name and then explicitly apply the named relation.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners, ICLR
finding: Asking the model to recall related problems and knowledge before solving beat 0-shot and few-shot chain of thought.
numbers: Codeforces: GPT-3.5-turbo Acc@1 of 15% with the best variant, level with GPT-4 at 16% (stated in the paper text). GSM8K and MATH gains of a few points for GPT-3.5-turbo, larger for text-davinci-003 and PaLM2; table columns could not be cleanly parsed so exact pairing is not recorded.
limits: Table layout lost in text extraction. No test of naming the relation itself.
agent_relevance: Self-generated recall of similar cases works. Add relation naming to the cue to make retrieval relation-based.

source: Moskvichev, Odouard & Mitchell (2023) The ConceptARC benchmark
finding: Humans solved spatial and semantic concept tasks far better than GPT-4 and top ARC programs, including relational concept groups.
numbers: Per-concept accuracy humans vs GPT-4: Above and Below .90 vs .23; Same and Different .93 vs .20; Inside and Outside .83 vs .27; Count .86 vs .03; Order .95 vs .23. Top ARC program 1 ranged .23-.77.
limits: GPT-4 text prompts in 2023, grid format. Later models not checked here.
agent_relevance: Relational concepts with everyday names (above, same, inside) are not reliably used by a model without scaffolding. Knowing the word is not the ability.

source: Relational reasoning and educational applications (Behavioral Sciences, 2026)
finding: Review states that relational mindset must be induced before encoding to help retrieval, and that relational language improves performance on specific tasks.
numbers: Cites Goldwater & Jamrozik (2019): relational mindset boosts retrieval of analogies from several texts only if elicited before encoding. States that with more knowledge students map on relations, not surface (Loewenstein & Gentner, 2005).
limits: Review, second-hand. No full effect size list extracted.
agent_relevance: Timing matters: prompt for relations before the agent reads or encodes, not after.

source: Semantic anchors facilitate task encoding in continual learning (Open Mind, 2025)
finding: Semantically rich task labels and response labels reduced forgetting versus meaningless shape labels across four experiments.
numbers: Abstract only. Experiments 1-4; modelled with RNNs and reinforcement learning. Numbers not read.
limits: Humans, task rules. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Meaningful names for steps or rules reduce interference between tasks. Use meaningful operator names.

source: Verbal recoding underlies visual ambiguity resolution, even in a nonlinguistic context (J. Exp. Psychol. Gen., 2026)
finding: Phonological interference reduced a sequence-order categorisation effect; visuospatial interference did not. People appear to recode abstract shapes as words.
numbers: Abstract only. Numbers not read.
limits: Abstract only. Different task, but shows spontaneous naming.
agent_relevance: Spontaneous naming is a default human strategy. Blocking it is a useful ablation for an agent.

source: Mahowald et al. (2024) Dissociating language and thought in large language models
finding: Distinguishes formal from functional linguistic competence in LLMs. Strong formal competence, uneven reasoning competence.
numbers: Search listing only; not opened.
limits: Not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Fluent relation talk in an LLM does not guarantee relational reasoning.

source: Synthesis of boundary conditions from sources read
finding: Label effects are clearest when labels invite comparison across cases and shape encoding. They are weaker for perceptually distinct categories (failed replication of Lupyan 2007) and absent for unseen-object perception (EEG null).
numbers: Mind Melds Exp 2: categoricality effect vs no-labels ns. Redundant-label replication: failed. Cortex 2026: null with N=20.
limits: Synthesis across sources; several only abstract-checked.
agent_relevance: Evidence supports labels for comparison and retrieval; it does not support them as a general performance booster.
